claim: Grid cells exhibit firing fields that are arranged in a triangular grid pattern when subjects navigate through spatial environments.
source: When subjects navigate through spatial environments, grid cells exhibit firing fields that are arranged in a triangular grid pattern.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by citations to foundational work (Hafting et al., 2005; Jacobs et al., 2013) and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: Direct recordings of grid cells from the human brain are rare.
source: Direct recordings of grid cells from the human brain are rare.
evidence: This statement reflects the practical limitations of invasive recording methods in humans, supported by citations to rare human studies (Jacobs et al., 2013; Nadasdy et al., 2017).

claim: fMRI studies proposed an indirect measure of entorhinal grid-cell activity, quantified as hexadirectional modulation of fMRI activity as a function of the subject's movement direction.
source: Hence, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies proposed an indirect measure of entorhinal grid-cell activity, quantified as hexadirectional modulation of fMRI activity as a function of the subject's movement direction.
evidence: This is supported by citations to fMRI studies (Doeller et al., 2010) that developed this methodology.

claim: It remains unclear how the activity of a population of grid cells may exhibit hexadirectional modulation.
source: However, it remains unclear how the activity of a population of grid cells may exhibit hexadirectional modulation.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current understanding, which is the motivation for the study.

claim: Hexadirectional modulation is best explained by head-direction tuning aligned to the grid axes.
source: Here, we use numerical simulations and analytical calculations to suggest that this hexadirectional modulation is best explained by head-direction tuning aligned to the grid axes, whereas it is not clearly supported by a bias of grid cells toward a particular phase offset.
evidence: This claim is supported by the numerical simulations and analytical calculations presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 2 and Figure 5.

claim: Hexadirectional modulation is not clearly supported by a bias of grid cells toward a particular phase offset.
source: Here, we use numerical simulations and analytical calculations to suggest that this hexadirectional modulation is best explained by head-direction tuning aligned to the grid axes, whereas it is not clearly supported by a bias of grid cells toward a particular phase offset.
evidence: This is supported by simulations showing that realistic clustering parameters result in substantially reduced hexasymmetries (Figure 4, Figure 5).

claim: Firing-rate adaptation can result in hexadirectional modulation.
source: Firing-rate adaptation can result in hexadirectional modulation, but the available cellular data is insufficient to clearly support or refute this option.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations in Figure 3, showing that repetition suppression can produce hexadirectional modulation under certain conditions.

claim: The available cellular data is insufficient to clearly support or refute the firing-rate adaptation hypothesis.
source: Firing-rate adaptation can result in hexadirectional modulation, but the available cellular data is insufficient to clearly support or refute this option.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of empirical evidence regarding adaptation parameters in grid cells.

claim: The magnitude of hexadirectional modulation depends considerably on the subject's navigation pattern.
source: The magnitude of hexadirectional modulation furthermore depends considerably on the subject's navigation pattern, indicating that future fMRI studies could be designed to test which hypothesis most likely accounts for the fMRI measure of grid cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations comparing star-like walks, piecewise linear walks, and random walks across all three hypotheses (Figures 2-5).

claim: Place cells were discovered by O'Keefe and Dostrovsky in 1971.
source: The neural basis of spatial navigation comprises multiple specialized cell types such as place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971), head-direction (HD) cells (Taube et al., 1990), and grid cells (Hafting et al., 2005), whose activity profiles result from intricate mechanisms of microcircuits in the medial temporal lobes (Tukker et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by the citation to the original discovery paper.

claim: Head-direction cells were discovered by Taube et al. in 1990.
source: The neural basis of spatial navigation comprises multiple specialized cell types such as place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971), head-direction (HD) cells (Taube et al., 1990), and grid cells (Hafting et al., 2005), whose activity profiles result from intricate mechanisms of microcircuits in the medial temporal lobes (Tukker et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by the citation to the original discovery paper.

claim: Grid cells were discovered by Hafting et al. in 2005.
source: The neural basis of spatial navigation comprises multiple specialized cell types such as place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971), head-direction (HD) cells (Taube et al., 1990), and grid cells (Hafting et al., 2005), whose activity profiles result from intricate mechanisms of microcircuits in the medial temporal lobes (Tukker et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by the citation to the original discovery paper.

claim: Grid cells activate whenever an animal or human traverses the vertices of a triangular grid tiling the entire environment into equilateral triangles.
source: Grid cells are neurons that activate whenever an animal or human traverses the vertices of a triangular grid tiling the entire environment into equilateral triangles (Hafting et al., 2005; Jacobs et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a fundamental property of grid cells supported by citations to empirical studies in both animals and humans.

claim: Grid cells may allow the navigating organism to perform vector computations.
source: Grid cells may allow the navigating organism to perform vector computations and may thus constitute an essential neural substrate for different types of spatial navigation including path integration, though their exact functional role still remains unclear (Stemmler et al., 2015; Bush et al., 2015; Moser et al., 2017; Stangl et al., 2018; Gil et al., 2018; Banino et al., 2018; Bierbrauer et al., 2020; Ginosar et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal about grid cell function supported by multiple citations, though the authors note the exact role remains unclear.

claim: The exact functional role of grid cells still remains unclear.
source: Grid cells may allow the navigating organism to perform vector computations and may thus constitute an essential neural substrate for different types of spatial navigation including path integration, though their exact functional role still remains unclear (Stemmler et al., 2015; Bush et al., 2015; Moser et al., 2017; Stangl et al., 2018; Gil et al., 2018; Banino et al., 2018; Bierbrauer et al., 2020; Ginosar et al., 2023).
evidence: This acknowledges the current state of uncertainty in the field despite multiple studies.

claim: In rodents, grid cells can be recorded using electrodes inserted into the medial entorhinal cortex.
source: In rodents, grid cells can be recorded using electrodes inserted into the medial entorhinal cortex (EC).
evidence: This is a standard methodological approach in rodent neuroscience, representing established knowledge.

claim: In humans, measuring grid cells using invasive methods is only rarely possible, e.g., by recording single-neuron activity in epilepsy patients who are neurosurgically implanted with intracranial depth electrodes.
source: In humans, measuring grid cells using invasive methods is only rarely possible, e.g., by recording single-neuron activity in epilepsy patients who are neurosurgically implanted with intracranial depth electrodes (Jacobs et al., 2013; Nadasdy et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the practical and ethical limitations of invasive recordings in humans, supported by citations to rare human studies.

claim: A functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) method has been developed that tests for a hexadirectional modulation of the blood-oxygen-level-dependent signal as a function of the subject's movement direction through a virtual environment.
source: Hence, to enable the detection of grid cells in healthy humans, a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) method has been developed that tests for a hexadirectional modulation of the blood-oxygen-level-dependent signal as a function of the subject's movement direction through a virtual environment (Doeller et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes a methodological innovation supported by citation to the original study.

claim: The phenomenon of hexadirectional modulation of the fMRI signal has been replicated repeatedly in recent years.
source: We here refer to this phenomenon of a hexadirectional modulation of the fMRI signal as 'macroscopic grid-like representations', which has been replicated repeatedly in recent years (e.g. Kunz et al., 2015; Bellmund et al., 2016; Horner et al., 2016; Constantinescu et al., 2016; Bierbrauer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple replication studies.

claim: The mechanisms underlying the emergence of macroscopic grid-like representations remain still unclear.
source: The mechanisms underlying the emergence of such macroscopic grid-like representations remain still unclear, however.
evidence: This identifies the knowledge gap that motivates the current study.

claim: Three main hypotheses have been developed to explain macroscopic grid-like representations: (i) the 'conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis'; (ii) the 'repetition suppression hypothesis'; and (iii) the 'structure-function mapping hypothesis'.
source: Three main hypotheses have been developed: (i) the 'conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis'; (ii) the 'repetition suppression hypothesis'; and (iii) the 'structure-function mapping hypothesis' (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work (Doeller et al., 2010; Kunz et al., 2019) and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Conjunctive grid by head-direction cells were found in the deeper layers of the entorhinal cortex and in pre- and parasubiculum.
source: The conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis rests on two key findings: first, the existence of conjunctive grid by HD cells, which were found in the deeper layers of the entorhinal cortex and in pre- and parasubiculum (Sargolini et al., 2006); second, the observation that the directional tuning of grid cells within the entorhinal cortex is aligned with the grid axes (Doeller et al., 2010), though further studies are needed to corroborate this observation.
evidence: This is an empirical finding supported by citation to the original study.

claim: The directional tuning of grid cells within the entorhinal cortex is aligned with the grid axes.
source: The conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis rests on two key findings: first, the existence of conjunctive grid by HD cells, which were found in the deeper layers of the entorhinal cortex and in pre- and parasubiculum (Sargolini et al., 2006); second, the observation that the directional tuning of grid cells within the entorhinal cortex is aligned with the grid axes (Doeller et al., 2010), though further studies are needed to corroborate this observation.
evidence: This is an empirical observation supported by citation, though the authors note it needs further corroboration.

claim: Further studies are needed to corroborate the observation that directional tuning of grid cells is aligned with the grid axes.
source: The conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis rests on two key findings: first, the existence of conjunctive grid by HD cells, which were found in the deeper layers of the entorhinal cortex and in pre- and parasubiculum (Sargolini et al., 2006); second, the observation that the directional tuning of grid cells within the entorhinal cortex is aligned with the grid axes (Doeller et al., 2010), though further studies are needed to corroborate this observation.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of evidence and a call for future research.

claim: Movements aligned with the grid axes result in increased spiking activity of the conjunctive grid by HD cell population compared to misaligned movements, assuming the directional tuning width is not too broad.
source: Assuming that the directional tuning width of these conjunctive grid by HD cells is not too broad, movements aligned with the grid axes (as compared to misaligned movements) result in increased spiking activity of the conjunctive grid by HD cell population.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the properties of conjunctive cells, which is tested in the simulations (Figure 2).

claim: The systematic difference in the firing of conjunctive grid by HD cells when moving aligned versus misaligned with the grid axes may cause a macroscopically visible fMRI signal with hexadirectional modulation, given some correlation between population spiking activity and the fMRI signal.
source: Given some correlation between population spiking activity and the fMRI signal, this systematic difference in the firing of conjunctive grid by HD cells when moving aligned versus misaligned with the grid axes may thus cause a macroscopically visible fMRI signal with hexadirectional modulation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 1B and tested through simulations.

claim: The conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis does not necessarily depend on an alignment between the preferred head directions with the grid axes.
source: We note that the conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis does not necessarily depend on an alignment between the preferred head directions with the grid axes.
evidence: This is a clarification about the theoretical requirements of the hypothesis.

claim: The repetition suppression hypothesis is based on the assumption that the phenomenon of repetition suppression also applies to grid cells.
source: The repetition suppression hypothesis (Figure 1C) is based on the assumption that the phenomenon of repetition suppression—i.e., neural activity being reduced for repeated stimuli (Grill-Spector et al., 2006)—also applies to grid cells (Doeller et al., 2010; Killian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on repetition suppression in general and its potential application to grid cells.

claim: Relatively fewer different grid cells are activated more often during movements aligned with the grid axes, and relatively more different grid cells are activated less often during misaligned movements.
source: Critical to this hypothesis is that relatively fewer different grid cells are activated more often during movements aligned with the grid axes, and relatively more different grid cells are activated less often during misaligned movements.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about grid cell activation patterns that is illustrated in Figure 1C and tested in simulations (Figure 3).

claim: A higher degree of repetition suppression at the level of spiking activity or the fMRI signal during aligned movements as compared with misaligned movements can emerge due to systematic differences in how many grid cells are activated how often, resulting in a hexadirectional modulation of fMRI activity.
source: Due to this systematic difference in how many grid cells are activated how often, a higher degree of repetition suppression at the level of spiking activity or the fMRI signal (i.e. fMRI adaptation) during aligned movements as compared with misaligned movements can emerge, again resulting in a hexadirectional modulation of fMRI activity as a function of the subject's movement direction through the spatial environment.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction tested through simulations in Figure 3.

claim: Studies in rodents have demonstrated that the firing fields of anatomically adjacent grid cells have similar spacing and orientation.
source: Regarding the structure-function mapping hypothesis (Figure 1D), studies in rodents have demonstrated that the firing fields of anatomically adjacent grid cells do not only have similar spacing and orientation (Stensola et al., 2012), but also a similar grid phase offset to a reference location (Heys et al., 2014; Gu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an empirical finding supported by citations to rodent studies.

claim: The firing fields of anatomically adjacent grid cells have a similar grid phase offset to a reference location.
source: Regarding the structure-function mapping hypothesis (Figure 1D), studies in rodents have demonstrated that the firing fields of anatomically adjacent grid cells do not only have similar spacing and orientation (Stensola et al., 2012), but also a similar grid phase offset to a reference location (Heys et al., 2014; Gu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an empirical finding supported by citations to rodent studies.

claim: Grid cells cluster anatomically.
source: Studies in rodents observed that grid cells also cluster anatomically (Obenhaus et al., 2022; Naumann et al., 2018), which may lead to stronger grid-like representations in some voxels (with an increased percentage of grid cells) than in others (with a decreased percentage of grid cells).
evidence: This is an empirical finding supported by citations to rodent studies.

claim: Anatomical clustering of grid cells may lead to stronger grid-like representations in some voxels than in others.
source: Studies in rodents observed that grid cells also cluster anatomically (Obenhaus et al., 2022; Naumann et al., 2018), which may lead to stronger grid-like representations in some voxels (with an increased percentage of grid cells) than in others (with a decreased percentage of grid cells).
evidence: This is a theoretical inference from the empirical finding of anatomical clustering.

claim: Recordings from a small area of the EC may sample grid cells with similar firing fields, which might show higher average firing rates during aligned movements versus misaligned movements.
source: Therefore, recordings from a small area of the EC (e.g. a sufficiently small voxel of an fMRI scan) may sample grid cells with similar firing fields, which basically behave similarly. It has been suggested that such a grid cell population might show higher average firing rates during aligned movements (because more firing fields are traversed) versus misaligned movements, again resulting in macroscopically visible grid-like representations (Kunz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by citation and tested in simulations (Figure 4).

claim: All three hypotheses can result in macroscopic grid-like representations under ideal and specific conditions.
source: Our results show that all three hypotheses can result in macroscopic grid-like representations under ideal and specific conditions, but that the strength of the hexadirectional modulation varies by orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is a key finding from the simulations presented in Figures 2-5.

claim: The strength of the hexadirectional modulation varies by orders of magnitude across the three hypotheses.
source: Our results show that all three hypotheses can result in macroscopic grid-like representations under ideal and specific conditions, but that the strength of the hexadirectional modulation varies by orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5, which compares hexasymmetry values across hypotheses.

claim: The subjects' type of navigation paths through the spatial environments and the exact biological characteristics of grid cells determine to what extent a given hypothesis can explain a hexadirectional population signal in the EC.
source: Key findings are also that the subjects' type of navigation paths through the spatial environments and the exact biological characteristics of grid cells determine to what extent a given hypothesis can explain a hexadirectional population signal in the EC.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the simulations comparing different trajectory types and parameter values (Figures 2-5).

claim: Star-like walks ensured that the navigation trajectory itself exhibited a hexasymmetry that was essentially zero.
source: During each path segment of star-like walks, the simulated agent started from the same (x/y)-coordinate and navigated along 1 of 360 predefined allocentric navigation directions (0° to 359° in steps of 1°; Figure 2B, left). This ensured that the navigation trajectory itself exhibited a hexasymmetry that was essentially zero.
evidence: This is a property of the star-like walk design, demonstrated in the simulations (Figure 2B).

claim: Each path segment in star-like walks had a length of 300 cm, which was 10 times the grid scale.
source: Each path had a length of 300 cm, which was 10 times the grid scale (see Table 1 for a summary of all model parameters).
evidence: This is a parameter choice documented in Table 1.

claim: For star-like walks, after each path segment was traversed, the agent was 'teleported' back to the initial (x/y)-coordinate and completed the next path segment.
source: After each path segment was traversed, the agent was 'teleported' back to the initial (x/y)-coordinate and completed the next path segment.
evidence: This describes the simulation procedure for star-like walks.

claim: Star-like navigation including teleportation is unusual for real-world experiments but can be implemented in virtual-reality experiments.
source: For real-world experiments, this type of navigation including teleportation is unusual, but it can be implemented in virtual-reality experiments (Vass et al., 2016; Deuker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies that have used teleportation in virtual reality.

claim: Piecewise linear walks consisted of 360 path segments of 300 cm length along the same 360 predefined allocentric navigation directions as in star-like walks, but the path segments were 'unwrapped' such that the starting location of a path segment was identical with the end location of the preceding path segment.
source: During piecewise linear walks, the subject also completed 360 path segments of 300 cm length along the same 360 predefined allocentric navigation directions, as in the star-like walks. In this case, however, the path segments were 'unwrapped' such that the starting location of a path segment was identical with the end location of the preceding path segment (Figure 2C, left).
evidence: This describes the simulation procedure for piecewise linear walks, illustrated in Figure 2C.

claim: The sequence of allocentric navigation directions in piecewise linear walks was randomly chosen.
source: The sequence of allocentric navigation directions was randomly chosen.
evidence: This describes a parameter of the piecewise linear walk simulation.

claim: Piecewise linear walks do not exhibit hexasymmetry a priori.
source: As for star-like walks, piecewise linear walks do not exhibit hexasymmetry a priori.
evidence: This is a property of the piecewise linear walk design by construction.

claim: Random walks were modeled following Kropff and Treves, 2008; Si et al., 2012; D'Albis and Kempter, 2017, which allowed variation of the tortuosity of the paths.
source: For random walks, we modeled navigation trajectories following Kropff and Treves, 2008; Si et al., 2012; D'Albis and Kempter, 2017 (for details, see Methods around Equation 1), which allowed us to vary the tortuosity of the paths.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach for random walks, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Tortuosity describes how convoluted a navigation path is, with higher tortuosity meaning more convoluted paths.
source: Tortuosity describes how convoluted a navigation path is (the higher the tortuosity, the more convoluted the path).
evidence: This is a definition of the tortuosity parameter.

claim: Random walks in finite enclosures (circles and squares) with different sizes and orientations had a negligible effect on path hexasymmetry.
source: Apart from random walks in basically infinite environments, we also simulated random walks in finite enclosures (circles and squares) with different sizes and orientations; we found that these restrictions had a negligible effect on path hexasymmetry (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C; for a definition of path hexasymmetry, see the paragraph after the next one).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Random walks exhibit varying degrees of path hexasymmetry because the allocentric navigation directions are not predefined.
source: Because the allocentric navigation directions are not predefined for random walks, they exhibit varying degrees of path hexasymmetry.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the random walk design.

claim: The longer the simulated random walks, the smaller the path hexasymmetry.
source: The longer the simulated random walks, the smaller the path hexasymmetry (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and derived analytically.

claim: The emergence of grid-like representations based on the conjunctive hypothesis is robust against the specific type of navigation strategy.
source: As we describe below, the emergence of grid-like representations based on the conjunctive hypothesis is robust against the specific type of navigation strategy, whereas the other two hypotheses are sensitive to particular navigation strategies.
evidence: This is a key finding from comparing the three hypotheses across different trajectory types (Figure 5).

claim: The repetition suppression and structure-function mapping hypotheses are sensitive to particular navigation strategies.
source: As we describe below, the emergence of grid-like representations based on the conjunctive hypothesis is robust against the specific type of navigation strategy, whereas the other two hypotheses are sensitive to particular navigation strategies.
evidence: This is a key finding from comparing the three hypotheses across different trajectory types (Figures 3-5).

claim: Future studies on hexadirectional signals should consider the kind of navigation paths subjects will use during a given task.
source: Future studies on hexadirectional signals should thus consider the kind of navigation paths subjects will use during a given task.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the finding that navigation type affects hexasymmetry.

claim: Conjunctive grid by HD cells with ideal values for HD tuning preciseness and alignment to grid axes resulted in clear hexadirectional modulation of sum grid-cell activity.
source: By modulating the activity of individual grid cells with an HD tuning term aligned with the grid axes (Methods, Equation 3), our simulations indeed showed that these properties resulted in a clear hexadirectional modulation of sum grid-cell activity (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Different types of navigation trajectories (star-like, piecewise linear, random) led to similar distributions of sum grid-cell activity as a function of movement direction and similar hexasymmetry values for the conjunctive hypothesis.
source: When considering different types of navigation trajectories, we found that they led to similar distributions of sum grid-cell activity as a function of movement direction and, accordingly, to similar hexasymmetry values (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations comparing trajectory types, shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: For the conjunctive hypothesis, the directions of maximal activity were aligned with the grid axes.
source: In all three cases, the directions of maximal activity were aligned with the grid axes.
evidence: This is a finding from simulations of the conjunctive hypothesis (Figure 2).

claim: The repetition suppression hypothesis proposes that grid-cell activity is subject to firing-rate adaptation, leading to reduced grid-cell activity when moving along the grid axes compared to other directions.
source: Next, we performed simulations to understand whether the repetition suppression hypothesis (Doeller et al., 2010) results in a hexadirectional modulation of population grid-cell activity. This hypothesis proposes that grid-cell activity is subject to firing-rate adaptation and thus leads to reduced grid-cell activity when moving along the grid axes as compared to when moving along other directions than the grid axes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the repetition suppression hypothesis, supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: When moving along the grid axes, the grid fields of fewer grid cells are traversed relatively more often (strong repetition suppression), whereas when moving not along the grid axes, the grid fields of more grid cells are traversed relatively less often (weak repetition suppression).
source: This difference is due to the fact that when the subject moves along the grid axes the grid fields of fewer grid cells are traversed relatively more often (strong repetition suppression), whereas when moving not along the grid axes the grid fields of more grid cells are traversed relatively less often (weak repetition suppression) (Doeller et al., 2010).
evidence: This explains the mechanism of the repetition suppression hypothesis, supported by citation.

claim: Star-like and piecewise linear walks resulted in clear and significant hexasymmetry values for the repetition suppression hypothesis.
source: When examining how the different types of navigation trajectories affected hexadirectional modulations based on repetition suppression, we found that star-like and piecewise linear walks resulted in clear and significant hexasymmetry values (Figure 3C and D), which is driven by the long linear segments in these trajectory types.
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The 30° shift in apparent preferred grid orientation for the repetition suppression hypothesis is due to the adaptation mechanism suppressing grid-cell activity more strongly when moving aligned with a grid axis compared to when moving misaligned.
source: This is due to the fact that the adaptation mechanism suppresses grid-cell activity more strongly when moving aligned with a grid axis as compared to when moving misaligned with a grid axis (Figure 3A).
evidence: This explains the mechanism behind the 30° shift, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: The pattern of sharp peaks at multiples of 60° for the structure-function mapping hypothesis is clearly distinct from the more sinusoidal modulation resulting from the conjunctive hypothesis and the more full-wave rectified sinusoidal modulation resulting from the repetition suppression hypothesis.
source: This pattern is clearly distinct from the more sinusoidal modulation of sum grid-cell activity resulting from the conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis (Figure 2) and the more full-wave rectified sinusoidal modulation resulting from the repetition suppression hypothesis (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a comparison of patterns across hypotheses, based on simulations in Figures 2-4.

claim: For the structure-function mapping hypothesis with piecewise linear walks and random walks, hexasymmetry appeared to be considerably lower compared to simulations with star-like walks.
source: When examining the structure-function mapping hypothesis for piecewise linear walks and random walks, hexasymmetry appeared to be considerably lower as compared to simulations with star-like walks (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: For the structure-function mapping hypothesis with piecewise linear walks and random walks, hexasymmetry values did not show a systematic dependency on the starting location of the subject's navigation trajectory relative to the locations of the grid fields.
source: For both piecewise linear walks and random walks, the hexasymmetry values did not show a systematic dependency on the starting location of the subject's navigation trajectory relative to the locations of the grid fields (Figure 4E and F, left), which is due to the fact that these navigation trajectories randomize the starting locations of all path segments.
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 4E and F, with an explanation of the mechanism.

claim: For the structure-function mapping hypothesis with piecewise linear walks and random walks, the apparent preferred grid orientations varied randomly as a function of the starting location of the very first path segment and did not exhibit systematic shifts.
source: Accordingly, the apparent preferred grid orientations varied randomly as a function of the starting location of the very first path segment and did not exhibit systematic shifts (Figure 4E and F, right), which is in contrast to the clear shifts in the apparent preferred grid orientations for star-like walks (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 4E and F, compared to Figure 4D.

claim: More realistic clustering concentration parameters resulted in substantially reduced hexasymmetries for the structure-function mapping hypothesis.
source: Accordingly, we found that these more 'realistic' clustering concentration parameters resulted in substantially reduced hexasymmetries for the structure-function mapping hypothesis (described in the next section and in Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: The neuronal hexasymmetries for realistic clustering parameters were much lower than those for the realistic conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis and for the realistic repetition suppression hypothesis.
source: Furthermore, the neuronal hexaysymmetries were much lower than the ones for the 'realistic' conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis and for the 'realistic' repetition suppression hypothesis.
evidence: This is a comparison of hexasymmetry values across hypotheses, shown in Figure 5.

claim: For piecewise linear walks in the structure-function mapping hypothesis, subsamples of path segments necessarily exhibit higher path hexasymmetries than the full set of path segments that has zero path hexasymmetry.
source: These subsamples of path segments necessarily exhibit higher path hexasymmetries than the full set of path segments that has zero path hexasymmetry.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of subsampling from a set with zero hexasymmetry.

claim: For piecewise linear walks in the structure-function mapping hypothesis, hexasymmetry values were driven by a subsampling of the movement directions due to the sparsity of the grid-field locations.
source: We thus conclude that, for piecewise linear walks, hexasymmetry values were driven by a subsampling of the movement directions due to the sparsity of the grid-field locations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of piecewise linear walks in the structure-function mapping hypothesis.

claim: The structure-function mapping hypothesis with very strong (ideal) clustering produces neural hexasymmetry values that are larger than expected from path hexasymmetries only with respect to star-like walks.
source: Taken together, the structure-function mapping hypothesis with very strong ('ideal') clustering produces neural hexasymmetry values that are larger than expected from path hexasymmetries only with respect to star-like walks, including a strong dependence on the subject's starting location (Figure 4D, left).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: The range of hexasymmetry values for the structure-function mapping hypothesis with ideal clustering is comparable to those of the repetition suppression hypothesis with ideal parameters.
source: This range of hexasymmetry values is comparable to those of the repetition suppression hypothesis with 'ideal' parameters (Figure 3), but values are at least an order of magnitude smaller than in the 'ideal' conjunctive grid by HD cell case (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a comparison of hexasymmetry values across hypotheses, based on Figures 2-4.

claim: Hexasymmetry values for the structure-function mapping hypothesis with ideal clustering are at least an order of magnitude smaller than in the ideal conjunctive grid by HD cell case.
source: This range of hexasymmetry values is comparable to those of the repetition suppression hypothesis with 'ideal' parameters (Figure 3), but values are at least an order of magnitude smaller than in the 'ideal' conjunctive grid by HD cell case (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a comparison of hexasymmetry values across hypotheses, based on Figures 2-4.

claim: When using realistic clustering concentration parameters, neural hexasymmetry values are further reduced compared to simulations with ideal clustering for the structure-function mapping hypothesis.
source: When using realistic clustering concentration parameters, neural hexasymmetry values are further reduced as compared to simulations with ideal clustering (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: For the conjunctive hypothesis, all three types of navigation led to significant neural hexasymmetries for both ideal and more realistic parameters.
source: For the conjunctive hypothesis, we found that all three types of navigation led to significant neural hexasymmetries. This was the case for both ideal parameters (Mann-Whitney U tests, all U=0, all p<0.001) and for more realistic parameters (Mann-Whitney U tests, all U=0, all p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical tests on simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: For the repetition suppression hypothesis, star-like walks and piecewise linear walks resulted in significant neural hexasymmetries for both ideal and weaker parameters.
source: For the repetition suppression hypothesis, we found that star-like walks and piecewise linear walks resulted in significant neural hexasymmetries for both ideal and weaker parameters (Mann-Whitney U tests, all U=0, all p<0.001), whereas random walks did not (Mann-Whitney U tests, both U>1753, both p>0.405).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical tests on simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: For the repetition suppression hypothesis, random walks did not result in significant neural hexasymmetries.
source: For the repetition suppression hypothesis, we found that star-like walks and piecewise linear walks resulted in significant neural hexasymmetries for both ideal and weaker parameters (Mann-Whitney U tests, all U=0, all p<0.001), whereas random walks did not (Mann-Whitney U tests, both U>1753, both p>0.405).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical tests on simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: If the conjunctive hypothesis was true, fMRI studies should see a hexadirectional modulation of entorhinal fMRI activity for all three types of navigation paths.
source: If the conjunctive hypothesis was true, fMRI studies should thus see a hexadirectional modulation of entorhinal fMRI activity for all three types of the subjects' navigation paths.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the simulation results for the conjunctive hypothesis.

claim: If the repetition suppression hypothesis was true, fMRI studies should observe significant neural hexasymmetries only for star-like walks and piecewise linear walks with long enough segments, whereas random walks should not lead to significant neural hexasymmetries.
source: If the repetition suppression hypothesis was true, fMRI studies should thus observe significant neural hexasymmetries only for star-like walks and piecewise linear walks with long enough segments, whereas random walks (with large enough tortuosities, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) should not lead to significant neural hexasymmetries.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the simulation results for the repetition suppression hypothesis.

claim: For the structure-function mapping hypothesis, most hypothesis conditions resulted in significant neural hexasymmetries compared to path hexasymmetries for both ideal and more realistic parameters, except for random walks with more realistic parameters.
source: Regarding the structure-function mapping hypothesis, the statistical tests showed that most of the hypothesis conditions resulted in significant neural hexasymmetries as compared to the path hexasymmetries multiplied with the average population activities. This was the case for both ideal parameters (Mann-Whitney U tests, all U<736, all p<0.001) and more realistic parameters (Mann-Whitney U tests for star-like walks and piecewise linear walks, all U=0, all p<0.001). Only the hypothesis condition with random walks and more realistic parameters exhibited no significant neural hexasymmetries (Mann-Whitney U test, U=1786, p=0.472).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical tests on simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The results regarding the structure-function mapping hypothesis should be treated with great caution because the neural hexasymmetries for star-like walks heavily depend on the starting location and different starting locations lead to different apparent grid orientations.
source: However, these results regarding the structure-function mapping hypothesis should be treated with great caution. First, the neural hexasymmetries for star-like walks heavily depend on the starting location of the subject relative to the grid fields, and different starting locations lead to different apparent grid orientations (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a cautionary note based on findings shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The significant results for the structure-function mapping hypothesis with piecewise linear walks and random walks actually result from an inhomogeneous sampling of movement directions through the grid fields and therefore do not reflect true neural hexasymmetries.
source: Second, the significant results for the navigation conditions with piecewise linear walks and random walks actually result from an inhomogeneous sampling of movement directions through the grid fields and therefore do not reflect true neural hexasymmetries (Figure 4T; see also Figure 5—figure supplement 2 for path hexasymmetry as a function of the number of subsampled path segments).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results shown in Figure 4T and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Only the structure-function mapping hypothesis is susceptible to the effect of inhomogeneous sampling because the grid fields are clustered at similar spatial locations.
source: Only the structure-function mapping hypothesis is susceptible to this effect because the grid fields are clustered at similar spatial locations (whereas the grid fields are homogeneously distributed in the case of the conjunctive hypothesis and the repetition suppression hypothesis).
evidence: This is an explanation of why the inhomogeneous sampling effect is specific to the structure-function mapping hypothesis.

claim: In simulations with infinitely long paths for the structure-function mapping hypothesis, the neural hexasymmetries for piecewise linear walks and random walks would not be significantly higher than the path hexasymmetries multiplied with the average population activities.
source: In simulations with infinitely long paths, the neural hexasymmetries (for the navigation types of piecewise linear walks and random walks) would not be significantly higher than the path hexasymmetries multiplied with the average population activities.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the analysis of the structure-function mapping hypothesis.

claim: In empirical studies, the effect of inhomogeneous sampling can be detected by correlating the subject-specific path distances with the subject-specific neural hexasymmetries: if there is a generally negative relationship, this will hint at the fact that the neural hexasymmetries are basically due to relevant path hexasymmetries of path segments crossing the grid fields.
source: In empirical studies, this effect can be detected by correlating the subject-specific path distances with the subject-specific neural hexasymmetries: if there is a generally negative relationship, this will hint at the fact that the neural hexasymmetries are basically due to relevant path hexasymmetries of path segments crossing the grid fields.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation for future empirical studies based on the simulation findings.

claim: The structure-function mapping hypothesis leads to true neural hexasymmetry only in the case of star-like walks.
source: In essence, we therefore believe that the structure-function mapping hypothesis leads to true neural hexasymmetry only in the case of star-like walks.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of the structure-function mapping hypothesis across trajectory types.

claim: For both circular and square environments, hexasymmetry strengths did not considerably depend on the size of the environment when the subject performed random walks.
source: Our simulations showed that for both circular and square environments, hexasymmetry strengths did not considerably depend on the size of the environment when the subject performed random walks (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Rotating the navigation trajectories relative to the grid patterns did not affect the hexasymmetry strengths.
source: Similarly, rotating the navigation trajectories relative to the grid patterns did not affect the hexasymmetry strengths (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Experiments in animals and humans can use various types and sizes of environments to investigate hexadirectional modulations of sum grid-cell activity.
source: These results thus suggest that experiments in animals and humans can use various types and sizes of the environments to investigate hexadirectional modulations of sum grid-cell activity.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future experiments based on the simulation findings about environment effects.
